danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Efter samtalen med sin kone rejste Pierre til Sankt Petersborg. Ved poststationen i Torzjok var der enten ingen heste, eller også ville postmesteren ikke stille dem til rådighed. Pierre måtte vente. Uden at klæde sig af lagde han sig på lædersofaen foran et rundt bord, lagde sine store fødder i deres overstøvler op på bordet og gav sig til at tænke.
»Skal portmanteauerne bringes ind? Og en seng gøres klar og te?« spurgte hans tjener.

Pierre svarede ikke, for han hverken hørte eller så noget. Han var begyndt at tænke over den forrige station og grundede stadig over det samme spørgsmål — et så vigtigt, at han ikke ænsede, hvad der foregik omkring ham. Han var ikke blot ligeglad med, om han kom til Petersborg tidligere eller senere, eller om han fik plads på denne station, men sammenlignet med de tanker, der nu optog ham, var det ham fuldstændig ligegyldigt, om han blev her i nogle timer eller resten af sit liv.

Postmesteren, hans kone, tjeneren og en bondekone, der solgte broderede varer fra Torzjok, kom ind i stuen og tilbød deres tjenester. Uden at ændre sin ligegyldige stilling så Pierre på dem hen over sine briller, ude af stand til at forstå, hvad de ville, eller hvordan de kunne fortsætte med at leve uden at have løst de problemer, der opslugte ham. Han havde været optaget af de samme tanker, siden den dag han vendte tilbage fra Sokolniki efter duellen og tilbragte den første pinefulde, søvnløse nat. Men nu, i rejsens ensomhed, greb de ham med særlig kraft. Ligegyldigt hvad han tænkte på, vendte han altid tilbage til de samme spørgsmål, som han ikke kunne løse og dog ikke kunne holde op med at stille sig selv. Det var, som om gevindet på den hovedskrue, der holdt hans liv sammen, var slidt ned, så skruen hverken kunne komme ind eller ud, men bare blev ved med at dreje nytteløst rundt på samme sted.

Postmesteren kom ind og begyndte underdanigt at bede hans Excellence om at vente blot to timer, hvorefter han under alle omstændigheder ville stille kurerhestene til hans Excellences rådighed. Det var tydeligt, at han løj og kun ville have flere penge af den rejsende.

»Er det godt eller dårligt?« spurgte Pierre sig selv. »Det er godt for mig, dårligt for en anden rejsende, og for ham selv uundgåeligt, fordi han har brug for penge til mad; manden sagde, at en officer engang havde givet ham en omgang prygl for at have ladet en privatrejsende få kurerhestene. Men officeren pryglede ham, fordi han skulle videre så hurtigt som muligt. Og jeg,« fortsatte Pierre, »skød Dolokhov, fordi jeg anså mig for krænket, og Ludvig XVI blev henrettet, fordi de anså ham for en forbryder, og et år senere henrettede de dem, der henrettede ham — også af en eller anden grund. Hvad er dårligt? Hvad er godt? Hvad bør man elske, og hvad bør man hade? Hvad lever man for? Og hvad er jeg? Hvad er livet, og hvad er døden? Hvilken magt styrer det hele?«

Der var intet svar på disse spørgsmål, undtagen ét, og det var ikke et logisk svar og slet ikke noget svar på dem. Svaret var: »Du vil dø, og alting ender. Du vil dø og vide alt eller ophøre med at spørge.« Men at dø var også frygteligt.

Gadesælgersken fra Torzjok fortsatte med klynkende stemme med at tilbyde sine varer, især et par gedeskindstøfler. »Jeg har hundredvis af rubler, jeg ikke ved, hvad jeg skal gøre med, og hun står i sin lasede kappe og ser frygtsomt på mig,« tænkte han. »Og hvad vil hun have pengene til? Som om de penge kan give hende bare en hårsbred mere af lykke eller sjælefred. Kan noget i verden gøre hende eller mig mindre hjælpeløse over for det onde og døden? — døden, der ender alt og må komme i dag eller i morgen — i hvert fald i et nu sammenlignet med evigheden.« Og igen drejede han skruen med det slidte gevind, og igen drejede den nytteløst rundt på samme sted.

Hans tjener rakte ham en halvskåret roman i brevform af Madame de Souza. Han begyndte at læse om lidelserne og de dydige kampe hos en vis Émilie de Mansfeld. »Og hvorfor gjorde hun modstand mod sin forfører, når hun elskede ham?« tænkte han. »Gud kan ikke have lagt en drift i hendes hjerte, der stred mod hans vilje. Min kone — som hun engang var — kæmpede ikke imod, og måske havde hun ret. Intet er fundet, intet er opdaget,« sagde Pierre igen til sig selv. »Alt, hvad vi kan vide, er, at vi intet ved. Og det er toppen af menneskelig visdom.«
Alt i og omkring ham syntes forvirret, meningsløst og frastødende. Men i selve denne modvilje mod alle sine omstændigheder fandt Pierre en slags pirrende tilfredsstillelse.
»Jeg tillader mig at bede Deres Excellence om at rykke lidt for denne herre,« sagde postmesteren, der kom ind i stuen fulgt af endnu en rejsende, der også var strandet på grund af mangel på heste.
Den nyankomne var en lille, bredbygget, gulbleg, rynket gammel mand med grå, buskede øjenbryn over klare øjne af en ubestemmelig grålig farve.

Pierre tog fødderne ned fra bordet, rejste sig og lagde sig på den seng, der var gjort klar til ham, idet han af og til kastede et blik på den fremmede, der med et dystert og træt ansigt møjsommeligt var ved at tage sit overtøj af med hjælp fra sin tjener, uden at se på Pierre. Med et par filtstøvler på sine tynde, knoglede ben og stadig iført en slidt, nankinbetrukket fåreskindskappe satte den rejsende sig på sofaen, lænede sit store hoved med de brede tindinger og korte hår tilbage og betragtede Bezukhov. Det strenge, kloge og gennemborende udtryk i det blik slog Pierre. Han følte trang til at tale med den fremmede, men da han havde besluttet sig for at stille et spørgsmål om vejene, havde den rejsende lukket øjnene. Hans rynkede, gamle hænder var foldet, og på fingeren af den ene så Pierre en stor støbejernsring med en segl, der forestillede et dødningehoved. Den fremmede sad ubevægelig, enten hvilende eller, som det forekom Pierre, hensunket i dyb og rolig meditation. Hans tjener var også en gul, rynket gammel mand uden skæg eller overskæg, tydeligvis ikke fordi han var barberet, men fordi det aldrig var vokset. Denne kvikke gamle tjener var ved at pakke den rejsendes sager ud og gøre te klar. Han bar en kogende samovar ind. Da alt var klar, åbnede den fremmede øjnene, rykkede hen til bordet, hældte te op til sig selv og til den skægløse gamle mand, som han rakte glasset. Pierre begyndte at føle uro og behovet, ja det uundgåelige i at indlede en samtale med denne fremmede.
Hans tjener bragte hans glas tilbage vendt på hovedet, med en halvgnavet sukkerklump, og spurgte, om der var brug for noget mere.
* For at vise, at han ikke ønskede mere te.
»Nej. Giv mig bogen,« sagde den fremmede.

Tjeneren rakte ham en bog, som Pierre antog var et andagtsskrift, og den rejsende fordybede sig i den. Pierre betragtede ham. Pludselig lukkede den fremmede bogen, lagde et bogmærke i den og lænede sig atter med armene på sofaens ryglæn tilbage i sin tidligere stilling med lukkede øjne. Pierre følte sig befippet og ønskede at undgå det blik, men de klare, gamle øjne tiltrak ham uimodståeligt.
Pierre følte sig forvirret og ønskede at undgå det blik, men de klare, gamle øjne tiltrak ham uimodståeligt.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: After his confrontation with his wife, Pierre left for Petersburg. At the Torzhok post station, either there were no horses or the postmaster refused to provide them. Pierre was forced to wait. Without undressing, he lay down on the leather sofa in front of a round table, put his big feet in their heavy boots up on the table, and began to think.
"Shall I bring in the bags? Get a bed ready? Some tea?" asked his valet.

Pierre didn't answer — he neither heard nor saw anything. He had started thinking at the last station and was still turning over the same question — one so important that he noticed nothing around him. Not only did it not matter whether he reached Petersburg sooner or later, or whether he found a room at this station, but compared to the thoughts consuming him it was all the same whether he stayed there a few hours or the rest of his life.

The postmaster, his wife, the valet, and a peasant woman selling Torzhok embroidery came into the room offering their services. Without changing his careless posture, Pierre looked at them over his spectacles, unable to understand what they wanted or how they could go on living without having solved the problems that absorbed him. He had been gripped by these same thoughts ever since the day he returned from Sokolniki after the duel and spent that first agonizing, sleepless night. But now, in the solitude of the journey, they seized him with special force. No matter what he thought about, he always came back to these same questions he could not solve yet could not stop asking himself. It was as if the thread of the main screw holding his life together had been stripped, so that the screw could neither go in nor come out, but just kept turning uselessly in the same place.

The postmaster came in and began obsequiously begging his excellency to wait only two hours, when — come what may — he would provide the courier horses. It was obvious he was lying and only wanted to squeeze more money out of the traveler.

"Is this good or bad?" Pierre asked himself. "It's good for me, bad for another traveler, and unavoidable for himself, because he needs money for food. The man told me that an officer once beat him for letting a private traveler have the courier horses. But the officer beat him because he needed to get somewhere quickly. And I," Pierre continued, "I shot Dolokhov because I felt insulted, and Louis XVI was executed because they considered him a criminal, and a year later they executed those who executed him — also for some reason. What is bad? What is good? What should one love, and what should one hate? What does one live for? And what am I? What is life, and what is death? What power governs everything?"

There was no answer to any of these questions, except one — and that was not a logical answer, not really a reply at all. The answer was: "You'll die and everything will end. You'll die and either learn everything or stop asking." But dying was terrifying too.

The Torzhok peddler woman, in a whining voice, kept offering her goods, especially a pair of goatskin slippers. "I have hundreds of rubles I don't know what to do with, and she stands there in her tattered coat, looking timidly at me," he thought. "And what does she want the money for? As if money could add even a fraction to happiness or peace of mind. Can anything in the world make her or me less vulnerable to evil and death? — death, which ends everything and must come today or tomorrow — in any case, in an instant compared to eternity." And again he twisted the stripped screw, and again it turned uselessly in the same place.

His servant handed him a half-finished epistolary novel by Madame de Souza. He began reading about the sufferings and virtuous struggles of a certain Emilie de Mansfeld. "And why did she resist her seducer when she loved him?" he thought. "God could not have placed in her heart a desire that went against His will. My wife — as she once was — did not resist, and perhaps she was right. Nothing has been found out, nothing has been discovered," Pierre told himself again. "All we can know is that we know nothing. And that's the height of human wisdom."
Everything within and around him seemed confused, senseless, and repulsive. Yet in this very disgust with all his circumstances, Pierre found a kind of bitter satisfaction.
"I must ask your excellency to move over a bit for this gentleman," said the postmaster, entering the room followed by another traveler, also stranded for lack of horses.
The newcomer was a short, large-boned, yellow-faced, wrinkled old man with bushy gray eyebrows hanging over bright eyes of an indefinite grayish color.

Pierre took his feet off the table, stood up, and lay down on a bed that had been prepared for him, glancing now and then at the newcomer. The old man, with a gloomy, tired expression, was wearily removing his wraps with his servant's help, not looking at Pierre. Wearing felt boots on his thin bony legs and keeping on his worn, nankeen-covered sheepskin coat, the traveler sat down on the sofa, leaned back his large head with its broad temples and close-cropped hair, and looked at Bezukhov. The stern, shrewd, penetrating expression of that gaze struck Pierre. He felt a desire to speak to the stranger, but by the time he had made up his mind to ask about the roads, the traveler had closed his eyes. His shriveled old hands were folded, and on one finger Pierre noticed a large cast-iron ring with a seal depicting a death's head. The stranger sat motionless, either resting or — as it seemed to Pierre — sunk in profound, calm meditation. His servant was also a yellow, wrinkled old man, without a beard or mustache — not because he was shaven but because they had never grown. This lively old servant was unpacking the traveler's canteen and preparing tea. He brought in a boiling samovar. When everything was ready, the stranger opened his eyes, moved to the table, and poured a glass of tea for himself and one for the beardless old man, to whom he passed it. Pierre began to feel a growing uneasiness and a sense that it was somehow necessary — even inevitable — to speak with this stranger.
The servant brought back his glass turned upside down, with an unfinished piece of nibbled sugar, and asked if anything else was needed.
* To indicate he didn't want more tea.
"No. Give me the book," said the stranger.

The servant handed him a book that Pierre took to be a devotional work, and the traveler became absorbed in it. Pierre watched him. Suddenly the stranger closed the book, put in a marker, and again leaned back on the sofa in his former position with his eyes shut. Pierre looked at him but didn't have time to look away before the old man opened his eyes and fixed his steady, severe gaze directly on Pierre's face.
Pierre felt flustered and wanted to avoid that look, but the bright old eyes drew him in irresistibly.
